top_concepts.label: ecosystem services
top_concepts.definition: Ecosystem services are the multitude of benefits that nature provides to society.

definitions.text: Ecosystem services are the multitude of benefits that nature provides to society.

narrower.label: cultural services
narrower.definition: Cultural services are ecosystem services that contribute to humans' emotional or social well-being, such as ecosystem components with spiritual significance, ecosystem components that contribute to aesthetic enjoyment, or ecosystems that offer options for recreation in nature.

definitions.text: Cultural services are ecosystem services that contribute to humans' emotional or social well-being, such as ecosystem components with spiritual significance, ecosystem components that contribute to aesthetic enjoyment, or ecosystems that offer options for recreation in nature.

narrower.label: provisioning services
narrower.definition: Provisioning services: Ecosystem services that provide humans with material objects, such as food, feed, fibre or water.

definitions.text: Provisioning services: Ecosystem services that provide humans with material objects, such as food, feed, fibre or water.

narrower.label: regulating services
narrower.definition: Regulation and maintenance services are ecosystem services that regulate biotic- or abiotic ecosystem components in a way that is beneficial for humans, such as climate regulation, pollination or disease control.

definitions.text: Regulation and maintenance services are ecosystem services that regulate biotic- or abiotic ecosystem components in a way that is beneficial for humans, such as climate regulation, pollination or disease control.

narrower.label: supporting services
narrower.definition: Providing living spaces for plants or animals and maintaining a diversity of plants and animals, are ‘supporting services' and the basis of all ecosystems and their services.

definitions.text: Providing living spaces for plants or animals and maintaining a diversity of plants and animals, are ‘supporting services' and the basis of all ecosystems and their services.

top_concepts.label: geology
top_concepts.definition: Geology refers to the underlying geological composition of an area, including rock types, mineral content, and geological processes. The geology of a region influences soil formation, structure, fertility, and drainage properties. Source: AGI, 'Encyclopedia of Geology'

definitions.text: Geology refers to the underlying geological composition of an area, including rock types, mineral content, and geological processes. The geology of a region influences soil formation, structure, fertility, and drainage properties. Source: AGI, 'Encyclopedia of Geology'

narrower.label: lithology
narrower.definition: Lithology refers to the physical characteristics of the parent material, such as the mineral composition, texture, and structure of the underlying rocks or sediments. The lithology of an area influences soil formation by affecting drainage, nutrient content, and the ability of the soil to support vegetation. Source: AGI, 'Encyclopedia of Geology'

definitions.text: Lithology refers to the physical characteristics of the parent material, such as the mineral composition, texture, and structure of the underlying rocks or sediments. The lithology of an area influences soil formation by affecting drainage, nutrient content, and the ability of the soil to support vegetation. Source: AGI, 'Encyclopedia of Geology'

narrower.label: alluvium
narrower.definition: Deposit made by a river or running water, often very productive agricultural soil.

definitions.text: Deposit made by a river or running water, often very productive agricultural soil.

narrower.label: colluvium
narrower.definition: Layered and heterogeneous sediment in local sinks or foodslopes based on relocated upslope soil material. Occurs often in agricultural landscapes.It is deposited by water and/or tillage erosion and often show higher contents in soil organic carbon.

definitions.text: Layered and heterogeneous sediment in local sinks or foodslopes based on relocated upslope soil material. Occurs often in agricultural landscapes.It is deposited by water and/or tillage erosion and often show higher contents in soil organic carbon.

narrower.label: gravel
narrower.definition: Gravel is a mineral granular material which does not stick together when wet and remoulded (i.e., noncohesive) and where the combined weight of 50% of the particles is larger than 4.75mm but smaller than 75mm with less than 15% of material smaller than 75µm.

definitions.text: Gravel is a mineral granular material which does not stick together when wet and remoulded (i.e., noncohesive) and where the combined weight of 50% of the particles is larger than 4.75mm but smaller than 75mm with less than 15% of material smaller than 75µm.

narrower.label: loess
narrower.definition: Aeolian, unlayered sediment which consists mainly of silt and fine sand.

definitions.text: Aeolian, unlayered sediment which consists mainly of silt and fine sand.

narrower.label: parent deposition
narrower.definition: Parent Deposition refers to the accumulation of materials, such as sediments or volcanic ash, that contribute to soil formation. These parent materials are deposited through natural processes such as erosion, weathering, or sediment transport, influencing soil texture, nutrient content, and water retention properties. Source: USDA NRCS, 'Soil Genesis and Classification'

definitions.text: Parent Deposition refers to the accumulation of materials, such as sediments or volcanic ash, that contribute to soil formation. These parent materials are deposited through natural processes such as erosion, weathering, or sediment transport, influencing soil texture, nutrient content, and water retention properties. Source: USDA NRCS, 'Soil Genesis and Classification'

narrower.label: parent lithology
narrower.definition: Parent Lithology is the specific geological composition of the parent material (e.g., bedrock or sediment) from which the soil develops. The mineral content and texture of this material directly affect the physical and chemical properties of the soil, such as fertility, permeability, and soil depth. Source: USDA NRCS, 'Soil Genesis and Classification'

definitions.text: Parent Lithology is the specific geological composition of the parent material (e.g., bedrock or sediment) from which the soil develops. The mineral content and texture of this material directly affect the physical and chemical properties of the soil, such as fertility, permeability, and soil depth. Source: USDA NRCS, 'Soil Genesis and Classification'

narrower.label: parent texture unconsolidated
narrower.definition: Parent Texture Unconsolidated refers to the texture of the unconsolidated parent material, such as loose sediments or debris, that has not been solidified into rock. This texture affects soil properties such as aeration, drainage, and root penetration, as well as its ability to retain nutrients. Source: USDA NRCS, 'Soil Genesis and Classification'

definitions.text: Parent Texture Unconsolidated refers to the texture of the unconsolidated parent material, such as loose sediments or debris, that has not been solidified into rock. This texture affects soil properties such as aeration, drainage, and root penetration, as well as its ability to retain nutrients. Source: USDA NRCS, 'Soil Genesis and Classification'

narrower.label: rock outcrop cover
narrower.definition: Rock Outcrops Cover measures the extent to which rock outcrops (exposed bedrock or rock masses) cover the landscape. The presence of rock outcrops can influence soil depth and water retention, as well as contribute to erosion and landscape stability, particularly in areas with minimal soil cover. Source: USDA NRCS, 'Soil Survey Manual'

definitions.text: Rock Outcrops Cover measures the extent to which rock outcrops (exposed bedrock or rock masses) cover the landscape. The presence of rock outcrops can influence soil depth and water retention, as well as contribute to erosion and landscape stability, particularly in areas with minimal soil cover. Source: USDA NRCS, 'Soil Survey Manual'

narrower.label: rock outcrop distance
narrower.definition: Rock Outcrops Distance quantifies the distance from a given point or area to the nearest rock outcrop. The proximity to rock outcrops can influence soil development, with areas closer to outcrops often having thinner soils and higher vulnerability to erosion. Source: FAO, 'Soil Formation and Classification'

definitions.text: Rock Outcrops Distance quantifies the distance from a given point or area to the nearest rock outcrop. The proximity to rock outcrops can influence soil development, with areas closer to outcrops often having thinner soils and higher vulnerability to erosion. Source: FAO, 'Soil Formation and Classification'

top_concepts.label: land cover
top_concepts.definition: The observed physical and biological cover of the Earth’s land surface including natural features such as vegetation, soils and waterbodies, as well as human-made features such as buildings and roads. Land cover is distinct from land use, which refers to the activities people undertake on a particular land cover type.

definitions.text: The observed physical and biological cover of the Earth’s land surface including natural features such as vegetation, soils and waterbodies, as well as human-made features such as buildings and roads. Land cover is distinct from land use, which refers to the activities people undertake on a particular land cover type.

narrower.label: plant cover
narrower.definition: Plants growing on the soil surface, typically compared with bare soil. This term can refer to existing flora, or that which is installed for erosion prevention, evapotranspiration, or carbon dioxide sequestration.

definitions.text: Plants growing on the soil surface, typically compared with bare soil. This term can refer to existing flora, or that which is installed for erosion prevention, evapotranspiration, or carbon dioxide sequestration.

narrower.label: root abundance
narrower.definition: The Roots Abundance describes the quantity of plant roots within a soil profile, typically categorized as few, common, or many. Root abundance reflects plant-soil interactions, soil fertility, and the physical structure that supports vegetation. Source: Soil Survey Manual (USDA, 2017).

definitions.text: The Roots Abundance describes the quantity of plant roots within a soil profile, typically categorized as few, common, or many. Root abundance reflects plant-soil interactions, soil fertility, and the physical structure that supports vegetation. Source: Soil Survey Manual (USDA, 2017).

narrower.label: root presence
narrower.definition: The Roots Presence identifies whether roots are visible in a soil profile or horizon. It indicates biological activity, soil health, and the suitability of the soil for plant growth. Roots are commonly observed during soil surveys and are classified by type and density. Source: Soil Survey Staff (2014). Keys to Soil Taxonomy.

definitions.text: The Roots Presence identifies whether roots are visible in a soil profile or horizon. It indicates biological activity, soil health, and the suitability of the soil for plant growth. Roots are commonly observed during soil surveys and are classified by type and density. Source: Soil Survey Staff (2014). Keys to Soil Taxonomy.

narrower.label: trees
narrower.definition: A woody perennial with a single main stem, or in the case of coppice with several stems, having a more or less definite crown.

definitions.text: A woody perennial with a single main stem, or in the case of coppice with several stems, having a more or less definite crown.

narrower.label: tree density
narrower.definition: Tree Density refers to the number of trees per unit area, usually expressed as trees per hectare. High tree density is often associated with forested ecosystems that contribute to soil fertility through organic matter inputs, root structures that stabilize the soil, and enhanced moisture retention. Source: FAO, 'Forest Resources Assessment'

definitions.text: Tree Density refers to the number of trees per unit area, usually expressed as trees per hectare. High tree density is often associated with forested ecosystems that contribute to soil fertility through organic matter inputs, root structures that stabilize the soil, and enhanced moisture retention. Source: FAO, 'Forest Resources Assessment'

top_concepts.label: physiography
top_concepts.definition: Physical geography (also known as physiography) is one of the three main branches of geography. Physical geography is the branch of natural science which deals with the processes and patterns in the natural environment such as the atmosphere, hydrosphere, biosphere, and geosphere.

definitions.text: Physical geography (also known as physiography) is one of the three main branches of geography. Physical geography is the branch of natural science which deals with the processes and patterns in the natural environment such as the atmosphere, hydrosphere, biosphere, and geosphere.

Physiography describes the physical characteristics of a landscape, including its landforms, slopes, and elevation. These features influence soil properties such as drainage, erosion, and moisture retention, helping to determine soil suitability for various land uses. Source: FAO, 'Soil Geography and Mapping'

narrower.label: landform complex
narrower.definition: Landform Complex describes a region with multiple interrelated landforms such as ridges, valleys, and hills. This property is essential for understanding how diverse landforms within a landscape influence soil distribution, water flow, and erosion patterns, ultimately affecting soil management strategies. Source: FAO, 'Soil Formation and Classification'

definitions.text: Landform Complex describes a region with multiple interrelated landforms such as ridges, valleys, and hills. This property is essential for understanding how diverse landforms within a landscape influence soil distribution, water flow, and erosion patterns, ultimately affecting soil management strategies. Source: FAO, 'Soil Formation and Classification'

narrower.label: major land forms
narrower.definition: Major Land Form refers to the significant physical features of the land, such as mountains, valleys, and plateaus, that influence soil development and landscape processes. These landforms shape the flow of water, sediment transport, and nutrient cycling, directly affecting the types of soils that form in different regions. Source: FAO, 'World Soil Resources Report'

definitions.text: Major Land Form refers to the significant physical features of the land, such as mountains, valleys, and plateaus, that influence soil development and landscape processes. These landforms shape the flow of water, sediment transport, and nutrient cycling, directly affecting the types of soils that form in different regions. Source: FAO, 'World Soil Resources Report'

narrower.label: slope
narrower.definition: The degree of steepness or incline of a position in the terrain.

definitions.text: The degree of steepness or incline of a position in the terrain.

narrower.label: slope forms
narrower.definition: Slope Form describes the shape or curvature of a slope, including its concave, convex, or straight profile. Slope form affects water runoff, erosion rates, and soil accumulation, influencing both the fertility and stability of the soil in hilly or mountainous regions. Source: FAO, 'Soil and Water Conservation'

definitions.text: Slope Form describes the shape or curvature of a slope, including its concave, convex, or straight profile. Slope form affects water runoff, erosion rates, and soil accumulation, influencing both the fertility and stability of the soil in hilly or mountainous regions. Source: FAO, 'Soil and Water Conservation'

narrower.label: slope gradient numeric
narrower.definition: Slope Gradient Property refers to the numerical measurement of the steepness of a slope, usually expressed as a percentage or angle. This property is crucial in determining soil erosion potential, water runoff, and suitability for land use, as steeper slopes are more prone to erosion and less suitable for cultivation without proper soil conservation measures. Source: USDA NRCS, 'Soil Erosion and Conservation'

definitions.text: Slope Gradient Property refers to the numerical measurement of the steepness of a slope, usually expressed as a percentage or angle. This property is crucial in determining soil erosion potential, water runoff, and suitability for land use, as steeper slopes are more prone to erosion and less suitable for cultivation without proper soil conservation measures. Source: USDA NRCS, 'Soil Erosion and Conservation'

narrower.label: slope orientation numeric
narrower.definition: Slope Orientation refers to the precise directional orientation of a slope, measured in degrees from a cardinal direction (e.g., 0° for north, 180° for south). The slope orientation impacts factors such as solar radiation, evaporation rates, and vegetation cover, all of which affect soil temperature, moisture retention, and erosion potential. Source: USDA NRCS, 'Soil Erosion and Landscape Analysis'

definitions.text: Slope Orientation refers to the precise directional orientation of a slope, measured in degrees from a cardinal direction (e.g., 0° for north, 180° for south). The slope orientation impacts factors such as solar radiation, evaporation rates, and vegetation cover, all of which affect soil temperature, moisture retention, and erosion potential. Source: USDA NRCS, 'Soil Erosion and Landscape Analysis'

narrower.label: slope pathways
narrower.definition: Slope Pathways identifies the natural flow paths of water, sediment, or other materials across a slope. These pathways, often defined by the topography, influence how water moves, erodes soil, and accumulates nutrients or contaminants. Understanding these pathways is critical for effective erosion control and water management in sloped areas. Source: FAO, 'Soil Erosion and Conservation'

definitions.text: Slope Pathways identifies the natural flow paths of water, sediment, or other materials across a slope. These pathways, often defined by the topography, influence how water moves, erodes soil, and accumulates nutrients or contaminants. Understanding these pathways is critical for effective erosion control and water management in sloped areas. Source: FAO, 'Soil Erosion and Conservation'

narrower.label: climate
narrower.definition: Climate is usually defined in a narrow sense as the average weather, or more rigorously, as the statistical description in terms of the mean and variability of relevant quantities over a period of time ranging from months to thousands or millions of years.

definitions.text: Climate is usually defined in a narrow sense as the average weather, or more rigorously, as the statistical description in terms of the mean and variability of relevant quantities over a period of time ranging from months to thousands or millions of years.

narrower.label: flood duration
narrower.definition: Flood Duration refers to the length of time during which an area is inundated by floodwaters. The duration of flooding can significantly affect soil structure, nutrient availability, and plant growth, especially in flood-prone regions. Source: USGS, 'Floodplain Management'

definitions.text: Flood Duration refers to the length of time during which an area is inundated by floodwaters. The duration of flooding can significantly affect soil structure, nutrient availability, and plant growth, especially in flood-prone regions. Source: USGS, 'Floodplain Management'

narrower.label: flood frequency
narrower.definition: Flood Frequency refers to how often flooding occurs in a particular area, typically expressed in terms of recurrence intervals (e.g., once every 10 years). This property is vital for assessing flood risk, soil erosion, and the potential for soil nutrient loss due to repeated flooding events. Source: USGS, 'Floodplain Management'

definitions.text: Flood Frequency refers to how often flooding occurs in a particular area, typically expressed in terms of recurrence intervals (e.g., once every 10 years). This property is vital for assessing flood risk, soil erosion, and the potential for soil nutrient loss due to repeated flooding events. Source: USGS, 'Floodplain Management'

narrower.label: water interchange
narrower.definition: The transfer of water between the principal water pools, forms, or environments of the hydrologic cycle.

definitions.text: The transfer of water between the principal water pools, forms, or environments of the hydrologic cycle.

narrower.label: evapotranspiration
narrower.definition: Process by which water is transferred from the land to the atmosphere by evaporation from the soil and other surfaces and by transpiration from plants.

definitions.text: Process by which water is transferred from the land to the atmosphere by evaporation from the soil and other surfaces and by transpiration from plants.

narrower.label: evapouration
narrower.definition: The conversion of water from the liquid state to the vapor state through the uptake of latent heat of vaporization.

definitions.text: The conversion of water from the liquid state to the vapor state through the uptake of latent heat of vaporization.

narrower.label: soil water evapouration
narrower.definition: The loss of water from bare soil to the atmosphere through conversion of liquid water to water vapor.

definitions.text: The loss of water from bare soil to the atmosphere through conversion of liquid water to water vapor.

narrower.label: overland flow
narrower.definition: The flow over the soil surface of rainfall or irrigation water that does not enter the soil matrix.

definitions.text: The flow over the soil surface of rainfall or irrigation water that does not enter the soil matrix.

narrower.label: precipitation
narrower.definition: (1) Liquid or solid products of the condensation or sublimation of water vapour falling from clouds or deposited from air on to the ground. (2) Amount of precipitation on a unit of horizontal surface per unit time.

definitions.text: (1) Liquid or solid products of the condensation or sublimation of water vapour falling from clouds or deposited from air on to the ground. (2) Amount of precipitation on a unit of horizontal surface per unit time.
Rain, snow, sleet, or hail that falls to or condenses on the ground.

narrower.label: fog
narrower.definition: Fog is a visible aerosol consisting of tiny water droplets or ice crystals suspended in the air at or near the Earth's surface.

definitions.text: Fog is a visible aerosol consisting of tiny water droplets or ice crystals suspended in the air at or near the Earth's surface.

narrower.label: hail
narrower.definition: Precipitation of particles of ice (hailstones). These can be either transparent, or partly or completely opaque. They are usually spheroidal, conical or irregular in form, and generally 5−50 mm in diameter. The particles may fall from a cloud either separately or agglomerated in irregular lumps.

definitions.text: Precipitation of particles of ice (hailstones). These can be either transparent, or partly or completely opaque. They are usually spheroidal, conical or irregular in form, and generally 5−50 mm in diameter. The particles may fall from a cloud either separately or agglomerated in irregular lumps.

narrower.label: rain
narrower.definition: Precipitation of liquid water.

definitions.text: Precipitation of liquid water.

narrower.label: sleet
narrower.definition: Precipitation of mixed rain and snow, mixed rain and hail or snow melting as it falls.

definitions.text: Precipitation of mixed rain and snow, mixed rain and hail or snow melting as it falls.

narrower.label: snow
narrower.definition: (1) Atmospheric precipitation of ice crystals. (2) Loose and porous aggregation of ice crystals or their fragments on any surface.

definitions.text: (1) Atmospheric precipitation of ice crystals. (2) Loose and porous aggregation of ice crystals or their fragments on any surface.

narrower.label: runoff
narrower.definition: Portion of rainfall, melted snow or irrigation water that flows across the grounds surface and is eventually returned to streams. Run-off can pick up pollutants from air or land and carry them to receiving waters.

definitions.text: Portion of rainfall, melted snow or irrigation water that flows across the grounds surface and is eventually returned to streams. Run-off can pick up pollutants from air or land and carry them to receiving waters.

narrower.label: surface runoff
narrower.definition: Water moving downslope over the soil surface as overland flow when water application exceeds infiltration into the soil.

definitions.text: Water moving downslope over the soil surface as overland flow when water application exceeds infiltration into the soil.

narrower.label: soil water infiltration
narrower.definition: The entry of water into the soil matrix through the air–soil interface.

definitions.text: The entry of water into the soil matrix through the air–soil interface.
infiltration of water into the soil

narrower.label: flux controlled water infiltration
narrower.definition: Water infiltration in which the water-supply rate determines the infiltration rate because water is applied more slowly than the soil's instantaneous infiltration rate.

definitions.text: Water infiltration in which the water-supply rate determines the infiltration rate because water is applied more slowly than the soil's instantaneous infiltration rate.

narrower.label: profile controlled water infiltration
narrower.definition: Infiltration in which soil water-transmission properties determine the actual infiltration rate and cumulative infiltration because the water-application rate exceeds the instantaneous infiltration rate.

definitions.text: Infiltration in which soil water-transmission properties determine the actual infiltration rate and cumulative infiltration because the water-application rate exceeds the instantaneous infiltration rate.

narrower.label: transpiration
narrower.definition: Transpiration consists of the vaporization of liquid water contained in plant tissues and the vapour removal to the atmosphere. Nearly all water taken up is lost by transpiration and only a tiny fraction is used within the plant.

definitions.text: Transpiration consists of the vaporization of liquid water contained in plant tissues and the vapour removal to the atmosphere. Nearly all water taken up is lost by transpiration and only a tiny fraction is used within the plant.

narrower.label: weather
narrower.definition: Weather refers to atmospheric conditions at a particular time in a particular location, including temperature, humidity, precipitation, cloudiness, wind, and visibility. Weather conditions do not happen in isolation, they have a ripple effect. The weather in one region will eventually affect the weather hundreds or thousands of kilometers away.

definitions.text: Weather refers to atmospheric conditions at a particular time in a particular location, including temperature, humidity, precipitation, cloudiness, wind, and visibility. Weather conditions do not happen in isolation, they have a ripple effect. The weather in one region will eventually affect the weather hundreds or thousands of kilometers away.

narrower.label: weather current
narrower.definition: Weather Conditions Current describes the current atmospheric conditions in a specific location, including factors like temperature, humidity, wind speed, and precipitation. These conditions directly affect soil moisture, temperature, and erosion rates, influencing soil fertility and the ability to support plant growth. Source: USGS, 'Meteorological and Soil Interactions'

definitions.text: Weather Conditions Current describes the current atmospheric conditions in a specific location, including factors like temperature, humidity, wind speed, and precipitation. These conditions directly affect soil moisture, temperature, and erosion rates, influencing soil fertility and the ability to support plant growth. Source: USGS, 'Meteorological and Soil Interactions'

narrower.label: weather past
narrower.definition: Weather Conditions Past refers to historical weather data, including past patterns of temperature, precipitation, and extreme weather events. Understanding past weather conditions helps in predicting soil behavior, erosion patterns, and agricultural productivity, as well as preparing for future changes in soil moisture and temperature. Source: USDA NRCS, 'Climate and Soil Interactions'

definitions.text: Weather Conditions Past refers to historical weather data, including past patterns of temperature, precipitation, and extreme weather events. Understanding past weather conditions helps in predicting soil behavior, erosion patterns, and agricultural productivity, as well as preparing for future changes in soil moisture and temperature. top_concepts.label: soil
top_concepts.definition: Loose and unconsolidated outer layer of the earth's crust, made up of small particles of different sizes.

definitions.text: Loose and unconsolidated outer layer of the earth's crust, made up of small particles of different sizes.
The uppermost layer of the Earth’s crust, supporting terrestrial life and forming the interface between the lithosphere and atmosphere.

narrower.label: fine soil
narrower.definition: Fine soil comprises all soilid compartments smaller than 2 mm.

definitions.text: Fine soil comprises all soilid compartments smaller than 2 mm.

narrower.label: rhizosphere
narrower.definition: Rhizosphere: region of soil near the roots of growing plants.

definitions.text: Rhizosphere: region of soil near the roots of growing plants.

narrower.label: soil skeleton
narrower.definition: Rock fragments within soil  which are larger than 2 mm

definitions.text: Rock fragments within soil  which are larger than 2 mm

narrower.label: subsoil
narrower.definition: A collective and general term for the layers of soil below the uppermost layer or topsoil. It can consist of sand, silt and clay but has little, if any, humus or other organic matter. Subsoil provides structure, holds moisture, and is a good foothold for rooting plants.

definitions.text: A collective and general term for the layers of soil below the uppermost layer or topsoil. It can consist of sand, silt and clay but has little, if any, humus or other organic matter. Subsoil provides structure, holds moisture, and is a good foothold for rooting plants.

narrower.label: topsoil
narrower.definition: Soil consisting of various mixtures of sand, silt, clay and organic matter; considered to be the nutrient-rich top layer of soil that supports plant growth.

definitions.text: Soil consisting of various mixtures of sand, silt, clay and organic matter; considered to be the nutrient-rich top layer of soil that supports plant growth.

narrower.label: crop class
narrower.definition: Crop Class refers to the categorization of land based on the type of crops cultivated. This property is used to assess soil management practices and land productivity, as different crops require specific soil conditions for optimal growth. Source: FAO, 'Guidelines for Soil Profile Description'

definitions.text: Crop Class refers to the categorization of land based on the type of crops cultivated. This property is used to assess soil management practices and land productivity, as different crops require specific soil conditions for optimal growth. Source: FAO, 'Guidelines for Soil Profile Description'

narrower.label: fragment class
narrower.definition: The Fragments Class categorizes the size, shape, and quantity of coarse fragments (e.g., gravel, stones) present in the soil. These fragments affect soil porosity, water retention, and root penetration. The classification includes gravelly, stony, or bouldery soils. Source: Soil Survey Manual (USDA, 2017).

definitions.text: The Fragments Class categorizes the size, shape, and quantity of coarse fragments (e.g., gravel, stones) present in the soil. These fragments affect soil porosity, water retention, and root penetration. The classification includes gravelly, stony, or bouldery soils. Source: Soil Survey Manual (USDA, 2017).

narrower.label: human influence class
narrower.definition: Human Influence Class classifies the extent of human impact on a landscape or ecosystem, ranging from minimal disturbance to high levels of modification. This classification helps in understanding the effects of urbanization, agriculture, or industrial activity on soil properties and ecosystem functions. Source: FAO, 'Land Degradation Assessment in Drylands'

definitions.text: Human Influence Class classifies the extent of human impact on a landscape or ecosystem, ranging from minimal disturbance to high levels of modification. This classification helps in understanding the effects of urbanization, agriculture, or industrial activity on soil properties and ecosystem functions. Source: FAO, 'Land Degradation Assessment in Drylands'

narrower.label: koeppen class
narrower.definition: Koeppen Class refers to the classification of climate zones based on temperature and precipitation patterns, as defined by the Köppen climate classification system. This classification directly influences soil temperature, moisture content, and vegetation types, which in turn affect soil formation and properties. Source: Köppen, W., 'Geiger's Climate Maps'

definitions.text: Koeppen Class refers to the classification of climate zones based on temperature and precipitation patterns, as defined by the Köppen climate classification system. This classification directly influences soil temperature, moisture content, and vegetation types, which in turn affect soil formation and properties. Source: Köppen, W., 'Geiger's Climate Maps'

narrower.label: land use class
narrower.definition: Land Use Class refers to the classification of land based on its primary use, such as agricultural, industrial, urban, or natural areas. This property helps assess the impact of land management practices on soil quality, including erosion risks, compaction, and fertility, and is critical for sustainable land-use planning. Source: FAO, 'Land Use and Land Cover Classification'

definitions.text: Land Use Class refers to the classification of land based on its primary use, such as agricultural, industrial, urban, or natural areas. This property helps assess the impact of land management practices on soil quality, including erosion risks, compaction, and fertility, and is critical for sustainable land-use planning. Source: FAO, 'Land Use and Land Cover Classification'

narrower.label: pedon
narrower.definition: A pedon is a three-dimensional body of soil that has sufficient area (roughly 1 to 10 m2) and depth (up to 200 cm) to be used in describing the internal arrangement of horizons and in collecting representative samples for laboratory analysis.

definitions.text: A pedon is a three-dimensional body of soil that has sufficient area (roughly 1 to 10 m2) and depth (up to 200 cm) to be used in describing the internal arrangement of horizons and in collecting representative samples for laboratory analysis.

narrower.label: porosity class
narrower.definition: The Porosity Class classifies soil by the proportion of pore spaces, typically expressed as a percentage. Classes include high, medium, or low porosity, influencing water and air movement in the soil. Source: Soil Science Society of America (SSSA) Glossary.

definitions.text: The Porosity Class classifies soil by the proportion of pore spaces, typically expressed as a percentage. Classes include high, medium, or low porosity, influencing water and air movement in the soil. Source: Soil Science Society of America (SSSA) Glossary.

narrower.label: profile description status
narrower.definition: The Profile Description Status indicates the level of detail and accuracy in documenting the features of a soil profile, including its horizons, texture, structure, and other observable characteristics. This property ensures that the soil profile description meets standards for completeness, enabling reliable classification and analysis. It is a critical aspect of soil studies, providing the basis for land-use planning, environmental assessment, and agricultural decision-making. narrower.label: slope gradient class
narrower.definition: Slope Gradient Class refers to the classification of slope steepness, such as flat, moderate, or steep, based on its angle. The gradient of a slope influences soil erosion rates, water drainage, and the suitability of land for agriculture, with steeper slopes typically being more prone to erosion. Source: USDA NRCS, 'Soil Erosion and Conservation'

narrower.label: slope orientation class
narrower.definition: Slope Orientation Class classifies the direction in which a slope faces (north, south, east, west) and can significantly affect local climate conditions, such as sunlight exposure, moisture, and temperature. For instance, south-facing slopes in the Northern Hemisphere receive more sunlight, influencing soil temperature, vegetation types, and soil moisture availability. Source: FAO, 'Soil and Water Conservation'

narrower.label: soil depth rootable class
narrower.definition: The Soil Depth Rootable Class classifies soils based on the depth of the rootable zone, which excludes impenetrable layers such as bedrock or compacted horizons. Soils are typically classified as shallow, moderately deep, or deep, depending on the depth of the root zone, which directly affects plant growth. Source: FAO (2006). Guidelines for Soil Description (4th ed.). Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations.

narrower.label: soil landscapes
narrower.definition: The full array of attributes that describe a distinct type of soil and its associated landscape, such as surface form, slope, water table depth, permafrost and lakes, is called a soil landscape.

definitions.text: The full array of attributes that describe a distinct type of soil and its associated landscape, such as surface form, slope, water table depth, permafrost and lakes, is called a soil landscape.

narrower.label: soil crusts
narrower.definition: A thin, dense layer on the soil surface characterized by low porosity, high density, and low permeability to air and water.

definitions.text: A thin, dense layer on the soil surface characterized by low porosity, high density, and low permeability to air and water.

narrower.label: soil biological crusts
narrower.definition: A soil-surface crust formed primarily by algal growth; also called a microbiotic crust.

definitions.text: A soil-surface crust formed primarily by algal growth; also called a microbiotic crust.

narrower.label: soil chemical crusts
narrower.definition: A crust formed on the soil surface by salt incrustation, as described for arid and semiarid regions.

definitions.text: A crust formed on the soil surface by salt incrustation, as described for arid and semiarid regions.

narrower.label: soil physical crusts
narrower.definition: A soil crust formed by alteration of soil structural properties, including structural and depositional crusts.

definitions.text: A soil crust formed by alteration of soil structural properties, including structural and depositional crusts.

narrower.label: soil depositional crusts
narrower.definition: A soil-surface crust formed by the transport and deposition of fine particles by surface flow.

definitions.text: A soil-surface crust formed by the transport and deposition of fine particles by surface flow.

narrower.label: soil structural crusts
narrower.definition: A soil crust formed by disruption of aggregates through raindrop impact and physicochemical dispersion of soil clays.

narrower.label: soil horizons
narrower.definition: In soil science: relatively uniform materials that extend laterally, continuously or discontinuously, throughout the pedounit; it runs approximately parallel to the surface of the ground and differs from the related horizons in many chemical, physical and biological properties.

definitions.text: In soil science: relatively uniform materials that extend laterally, continuously or discontinuously, throughout the pedounit; it runs approximately parallel to the surface of the ground and differs from the related horizons in many chemical, physical and biological properties.

narrower.label: A horizons
narrower.definition: The uppermost zone in the soil profile, from which soluble salts and colloids are leached, and in which organic matter has accumulated. Generally this represents the most fertile soil layer.

definitions.text: The uppermost zone in the soil profile, from which soluble salts and colloids are leached, and in which organic matter has accumulated. Generally this represents the most fertile soil layer.

narrower.label: B horizons
narrower.definition: B horizons form below an O, A, or E horizon and they have undergone sufficient changes during soil genesis, such that the properties of their original parent material are no longer discernible.

definitions.text: B horizons form below an O, A, or E horizon and they have undergone sufficient changes during soil genesis, such that the properties of their original parent material are no longer discernible.

narrower.label: C horizons
narrower.definition: The C horizon (parent material) is below the B Horizon. This layer is little affected by soil-forming processes and they thus have a lack of pedological development.

narrower.label: diagnostic horizons
narrower.definition: The diagnostic horizons at the soil surface are called epipedons (from the Greek 'epi, "over", and pedon, "soil"). The presence or absence of these particular diagnostic surface horizons help soil scientists determine the place of a soil within the Soil classification system.

narrower.label: spodic horizons
narrower.definition: The spodic horizon (from Gr. spodos, wood ash) is a dark coloured subsurface horizon which contains illuvial amorphous substances composed of organic matter and aluminium, with or without iron.

narrower.label: E horizons
narrower.definition: E (short for eluviated), is most commonly used to label a horizon that has been significantly leached of clay, iron, and aluminum oxides, which leaves a concentration of resistant minerals, such as quartz, in the sand and silt sizes.

narrower.label: hardpans
narrower.definition: A hardened soil layer in the lower A or in the B horizon caused by cementation of soil particles with organic matter or with materials such as silica or calcium carbonate. The hardness does not change appreciably with changes in moisture content, and pieces of the hard layer do not disintegrate in water.

narrower.label: organic horizons
narrower.definition: This layer generally forms above the mineral soil or occurs in an organic soil profile. The "O" stands for organic matter.

narrower.label: soil organic matter class
narrower.definition: The Soil Organic Matter Class classifies soil based on the amount and quality of organic matter it contains. Soils with high organic matter are usually fertile, retain moisture better, and support more biological activity. This classification helps in determining soil health and suitability for agricultural purposes. Source: Brady, N. C., & Weil, R. R. (2008). The Nature and Properties of Soils (14th ed.). Pearson Prentice Hall.

narrower.label: digital soil mapping
narrower.definition: Digital Soil Mapping (DSM) refers to techniques of mapping soils with mostly digital techniques, of course incorporating field (and traditional legacy soil information). DSM makes use of pedometrics which refers to the application of numerical techniques to describe and map soils. The idea is to make soil survey, classification, and land evaluation as objective as possible.

narrower.definition: Standardized guidelines define features and expressions of different soil parameters and characteristics, such as horizon names, soil types, soil color, or soil texture. This classification is typically divided into categories like slow, moderate, or rapid infiltration, based on how quickly water is absorbed into the soil. It is an essential property for understanding drainage, runoff, and irrigation needs. Source: Hillel, D. (2004). Introduction to Soil Physics. Academic Press.

narrower.label: subsoil

narrower.label: land use
narrower.definition: The activities, arrangements and inputs that people undertake on a particular land cover type to produce, change or maintain it. Land use encompasses a wide range of human activities, from farming and forestry to urban development and infrastructure, and is a key aspect of land management and sustainable development.

definitions.text: The activities, arrangements and inputs that people undertake on a particular land cover type to produce, change or maintain it. Land use encompasses a wide range of human activities, from farming and forestry to urban development and infrastructure, and is a key aspect of land management and sustainable development.

Land use corresponds to the socio-economic description (functional dimension) of areas: areas used for residential, industrial or commercial purposes, for farming or forestry, for recreational or conservation purposes, etc. Links with land cover are possible; it may be possible to infer land use from land cover and conversely. But situations are often complicated and the link is not so evident. Contrary to land cover, land use is difficult to 'observe'. For example, it is often difficult to decide if grasslands are used or not for agricultural purposes. Distinctions between land use and land cover and their definition have impacts on the development of classification systems, data collection and information systems in general.
The total of arrangements, activities, and inputs that people undertake in a certain land cover type (FAO, 1997a; FAO/UNEP, 1999).

narrower.label: land use bare cover
narrower.definition: Bare Cover Abundance refers to the extent of land area without vegetation or artificial cover, such as bare soil or rocky surfaces. High proportions of bare cover increase the risk of soil erosion and desertification, particularly in areas with poor vegetation or human disturbance. Source: FAO, 'Land Use and Land Cover Classification'

It is often quantified as the percentage of land area dominated by tree species, reflecting the ecological importance of forests in influencing soil fertility, moisture retention, and biodiversity. Forested areas typically contribute to soil formation and stabilization through leaf litter and root systems that reduce erosion. Source: FAO, 'Forest Resources Assessment'

Source: FAO, 'Grassland Ecosystems and Management'

They are also indicators of ecosystem health in many terrestrial environments. Source: FAO, 'Vegetation and Land Use in Arid Zones'

narrower.definition: Soil penetration resistance is a soil attribute that identifies areas with restrictions due to compaction, which results in mechanical impedance for root growth and reduced crop yield. narrower.definition: Biodrainage is defined as the process of removing the excess soil water through transpiration using bio-energy of the plant and radiation energy of the sun.

narrower.label: tile drainage
narrower.definition: Tile drainage is a form of agricultural drainage system that removes excess sub-surface water from fields to allow sufficient air space within the soil, proper cultivation, and access by heavy machinery to tend and harvest crops. The phrase "tile drainage" derives from its original composition from ceramic tiles of fired clay, which were similar to terracotta pipes yet not always shaped as pipes.

narrower.definition: The proportionality coefficient relating water flux density through soil to the hydraulic gradient; its value characterizes both the soil medium and the water and depends on the saturation or moisture state.

Hydraulic conductivity refers to the rate at which water moves through soil pores under a unit hydraulic gradient. It reflects the soil's ability to transmit water, influenced by texture, structure, and porosity. Soils with high hydraulic conductivity, like sandy soils, allow rapid water movement, while clayey soils exhibit slower water flow. This property is critical for understanding water infiltration, drainage, and irrigation management. Source: Brady, N.C., & Weil, R.R. (2017). The Nature and Properties of Soils.

narrower.label: soil conservation
narrower.definition: Soil conservation is a combination of all methods of management and land use that safeguard the soil against depletion or deterioration by natural or human-induced factors. It most often attempts to ensure that soil does not erode and wash into streams and lakes or blow away in the wind, but it also involves the protection of the soil from damage by machinery (e.g., compaction) or by harmful changes to its chemistry (e.g., acidification or salinization).

narrower.label: gully control
narrower.definition: Measures to control erosion in gulllies. Minimizing runoff volume and peak runoff rate through improved land use system is essential in gully control.

definitions.text: Measures to control erosion in gulllies. Minimizing runoff volume and peak runoff rate through improved land use system is essential in gully control.

narrower.label: soil conservation legislation
narrower.definition: The entirety of the laws, regulations and directives with legal effect in the area of ​​soil protection applicable to a country or a country community.

definitions.text: The entirety of the laws, regulations and directives with legal effect in the area of ​​soil protection applicable to a country or a country community.

narrower.label: soil drainage
narrower.definition: The removal of excess water from soil, through surface or subsurface pathways; under free drainage, gravity transfers the water from upper soil layers to lower layers.

definitions.text: The removal of excess water from soil, through surface or subsurface pathways; under free drainage, gravity transfers the water from upper soil layers to lower layers.

narrower.label: biodrainage
narrower.definition: Biodrainage is defined as the process of removing the excess soil water through transpiration using bio-energy of the plant and radiation energy of the sun.

definitions.text: Biodrainage is defined as the process of removing the excess soil water through transpiration using bio-energy of the plant and radiation energy of the sun.

narrower.label: controlled drainage
narrower.definition: A drainage system in which a control device intercepts water outflow to maintain the water table at a specified level below the soil surface.

definitions.text: A drainage system in which a control device intercepts water outflow to maintain the water table at a specified level below the soil surface.

narrower.label: conventional drainage
narrower.definition: Removal of excess water from the soil profile through perforated subsurface drainage pipes or tiles that discharge by gravity into a ditch or stream.

definitions.text: Removal of excess water from the soil profile through perforated subsurface drainage pipes or tiles that discharge by gravity into a ditch or stream.

narrower.label: pipe drainage
narrower.definition: Drainage using a buried pipe - regardless of material, size, or shape - which collects and conveys drainage water from a piece of land to a collector or to a main drain.

definitions.text: Drainage using a buried pipe - regardless of material, size, or shape - which collects and conveys drainage water from a piece of land to a collector or to a main drain.

narrower.label: subsurface drainage
narrower.definition: The removal of excess water and salts from soils via groundwater flow to the drains, so that the watertable and rootzone salinity are controlled.

definitions.text: The removal of excess water and salts from soils via groundwater flow to the drains, so that the watertable and rootzone salinity are controlled.

narrower.label: tile drainage
narrower.definition: Tile drainage is a form of agricultural drainage system that removes excess sub-surface water from fields to allow sufficient air space within the soil, proper cultivation, and access by heavy machinery to tend and harvest crops. The phrase "tile drainage" derives from its original composition from ceramic tiles of fired clay, which were similar to terracotta pipes yet not always shaped as pipes.

narrower.label: surface drainage
narrower.definition: The diversion or orderly removal of excess water from the surface of the land by means of improved natural or constructed channels, supplemented when necessary by the shaping and grading of land surfaces to such channels.

narrower.label: soil improvement
narrower.definition: Soil improvement concerns in the first place the appropriate management of problem soils. It also involves the improvement of degraded soils in terms of soil prevention, mitigation, and rehabilitation.

definitions.text: Soil improvement concerns in the first place the appropriate management of problem soils. It also involves the improvement of degraded soils in terms of soil prevention, mitigation, and rehabilitation.

narrower.label: land rehabilitation
narrower.definition: Land rehabilitation is an action to restore land already degraded to such an extent that the original use is no longer possible and the land has become practically unproductive.

definitions.text: Land rehabilitation is an action to restore land already degraded to such an extent that the original use is no longer possible and the land has become practically unproductive.

narrower.label: soil tillage
narrower.definition: The mechanical manipulation of soil to improve aeration, control weeds and incorporate organic matter.

definitions.text: The mechanical manipulation of soil to improve aeration, control weeds and incorporate organic matter.
Any physical loosening of the soil carried out in a range of cultivation operations, either by hand or mechanized.

narrower.label: conservation tillage
narrower.definition: An approach to soil management that excludes conventional tillage operations that invert the soil and bury crop residues. There are five types of conservation tillage systems: no-tillage (slot planting), mulch tillage, strip or zonal tillage, ridge tillage (including no-till on ridges) and reduced or minimum tillage.

There are five types of conservation tillage systems: no-tillage (slot planting), mulch tillage, strip or zonal tillage, ridge tillage (including no-till on ridges) and reduced or minimum tillage.
Tillage that leaves a high percentage of residues from previous crops on the soil surface.

narrower.label: minimum tillage
narrower.definition: Minimum tillage has been defined as the minimum soil disturbance needed for  crop production.

definitions.text: Minimum tillage has been defined as the minimum soil disturbance needed for  crop production.

narrower.label: no till
narrower.definition: A farming practice under which the soil remains largely undisturbed by farming operations.

definitions.text: A farming practice under which the soil remains largely undisturbed by farming operations.

narrower.label: ridge tillage
narrower.definition: Ridge  tillage or ridge-till describes  the practice  of  forming ridges from tilled soil into which widely spaced row crops are drilled. Such ridges may remain in place for several seasons while successive crops are no-tilled into the ridges,or they might be re-formed annually.

narrower.label: strip tillage
narrower.definition: Strip-till is a conservation system that uses a minimum tillage. It combines the soil drying and warming benefits of conventional tillage with the soil-protecting advantages of no-till by disturbing only the portion of the soil that is to contain the seed row.

definitions.text: Strip-till is a conservation system that uses a minimum tillage. It combines the soil drying and warming benefits of conventional tillage with the soil-protecting advantages of no-till by disturbing only the portion of the soil that is to contain the seed row.

narrower.label: stubble tillage
narrower.definition: A tillage system which retains a high percentage of crop residue on the soil surface, thereby reducing wind erosion.

definitions.text: A tillage system which retains a high percentage of crop residue on the soil surface, thereby reducing wind erosion.

narrower.label: deep tillage
narrower.definition: It is the tillage of the soil to a depth of 40-60 cm. It is done in the form of subsoiling and breaking up the plow furrow base.

definitions.text: It is the tillage of the soil to a depth of 40-60 cm. It is done in the form of subsoiling and breaking up the plow furrow base.

narrower.label: subsoiling
narrower.definition: Tillage of the subsoil or soil pan below the normal plough depth.

definitions.text: Tillage of the subsoil or soil pan below the normal plough depth.

narrower.label: disking
narrower.definition: Disking: Agricultural term to describe the process of using a disk, or harrow, to disturb the soil, setting back natural succession by cutting up grassy vegetation, thus preventing an area from maturing into briars, shrubs, and trees.

definitions.text: Disking: Agricultural term to describe the process of using a disk, or harrow, to disturb the soil, setting back natural succession by cutting up grassy vegetation, thus preventing an area from maturing into briars, shrubs, and trees.

narrower.label: nursery bed preparation
narrower.definition: Good nursery-bed preparation and forming is necessary to ensure accurate sowing of seed; good conditions for plant growth; the use of specialist machinery; and ease of harvesting. It involves preparing raised seedbeds of fine tilth, ensuring that soil fertility is correct, and controlling weeds or other pathogens.

narrower.label: planking
narrower.definition: Planking is done to crush the hard clods and to smoothen surface soil and to compact the soil lightly.

definitions.text: Planking is done to crush the hard clods and to smoothen surface soil and to compact the soil lightly.

narrower.label: ploughing
narrower.definition: Ploughing (tillage): mechanical cultivation of agricultural soils by the plough to different depths (20 – 30cm) deep, creating arable land.

definitions.text: Ploughing (tillage): mechanical cultivation of agricultural soils by the plough to different depths (20 – 30cm) deep, creating arable land.

narrower.label: deep ploughing
narrower.definition: Mixing of loose surface material by ploughing deeper than frequently done during annual soil cultivation.

definitions.text: Mixing of loose surface material by ploughing deeper than frequently done during annual soil cultivation.

narrower.label: primary tillage
narrower.definition: Primary tillage loosens the soil and mixes in fertilizer or plant material, resulting in soil with a rough texture.

definitions.text: Primary tillage loosens the soil and mixes in fertilizer or plant material, resulting in soil with a rough texture.

narrower.label: ripping (tillage)
narrower.definition: Ripping in tillage refers to the deep mechanical loosening of soil using specialized equipment, such as rippers or subsoilers.

definitions.text: Ripping in tillage refers to the deep mechanical loosening of soil using specialized equipment, such as rippers or subsoilers.

narrower.label: rotary cultivation
narrower.definition: A method of cultivation by a motorized cultivator that works the soil by means of rotating tines or blades.

definitions.text: A method of cultivation by a motorized cultivator that works the soil by means of rotating tines or blades.

narrower.label: secondary tillage
narrower.definition: Secondary tillage produces finer soil and sometimes shapes the rows, preparing the seed bed. It also provides weed control throughout the growing season during the maturation of the crop plants, unless such weed control is instead achieved with low-till or no-till methods involving herbicides.

definitions.text: Secondary tillage produces finer soil and sometimes shapes the rows, preparing the seed bed. narrower.label: seedbed preparation
narrower.definition: Tillage carried out after primary tillage and at shallower depths, to provide additional soil pulverisation, crop chemical mixing, soil surface levelling, firming and weed control,

narrower.label: soil puddling
narrower.definition: Physical manipulation of wet soil to slake and disrupt structural aggregates and decrease total porosity and macroporosity.

definitions.text: Physical manipulation of wet soil to slake and disrupt structural aggregates and decrease total porosity and macroporosity.
The tilling of flooded soil in order to create a muddy layer before seedlings are transplanted, especially for rice.

narrower.label: subsoiling
narrower.definition: Tillage of the subsoil or soil pan below the normal plough depth.

narrower.label: soil injection
narrower.definition: An application method in which a material entity is injected under pressure beneath the soil surface.

definitions.text: An application method in which a material entity is injected under pressure beneath the soil surface.

narrower.label: drainage to groundwater
narrower.definition: Continued downward movement of water through the soil profile after infiltration has ceased, where a shallow water table is present.

narrower.definition: The restriction of salt passage by soil pores when water is forced through the soil, while the pores permit water molecules to pass.

narrower.definition: Soil failure through crack formation, occurring when the energy released by a crack exceeds the increase in surface energy associated with the new surfaces.

narrower.label: soil hydrophobicity
narrower.definition: The water-repellent or non-wetting condition of soil in which soil particles repel water and the soil has a reduced affinity for water.

narrower.label: soil moisture hysteresis
narrower.definition: The dependence of the soil moisture-retention curve on the soil’s previous wetting and drainage history.

narrower.label: soil moisture redistribution
narrower.definition: The continued downward movement of water through a soil profile after infiltration ceases, by which wetted topsoil wets drier subsoil in the absence of a water table.

narrower.label: soil oxygen deficiency
narrower.definition: An insufficient supply of oxygen in soil for metabolic activities, including root respiration.

definitions.text: An insufficient supply of oxygen in soil for metabolic activities, including root respiration.

narrower.label: soil–plant–atmosphere continuum
narrower.definition: Soil–plant–atmosphere continuum is the near-surface environment in which water and energy transfer occurs from soil through plants to the atmosphere.

narrower.label: soil strain hardening
narrower.definition: A material property governing a gradual transition from elastic to plastic behavior under stress; soil under compactive stress may exhibit it as its structure changes.

definitions.text: A material property governing a gradual transition from elastic to plastic behavior under stress; soil under compactive stress may exhibit it as its structure changes.

narrower.label: soil water repellency
narrower.definition: The repulsion of water by soil particles.

definitions.text: The repulsion of water by soil particles.
Soil water repellency is a reduction in the rate of wetting and retention of water in soil caused by the presence of hydrophobic coatings on soil particles.

narrower.label: soil anthropogenic changes
narrower.definition: Activities, such as construction or drainage, which cause profound changes in the soil system.

definitions.text: Activities, such as construction or drainage, which cause profound changes in the soil system.

narrower.label: land take
narrower.definition: Land take entails the conversion of land to artificial surfaces, which impairs the valuable ecological functions of lands.

definitions.text: Land take entails the conversion of land to artificial surfaces, which impairs the valuable ecological functions of lands.

narrower.label: biological nitrogen fixation
narrower.definition: Conversion of atmospheric nitrogen (e.g. by bacteria in legume root nodules) into plant-usable form.

definitions.text: Conversion of atmospheric nitrogen (e.g. by bacteria in legume root nodules) into plant-usable form.
The process by which bacteria absorb nitrogen gas from the air and convert it to ammonium that plants can use.

narrower.label: bioturbation
narrower.definition: Bioturbation is the biogenic transport of sediment or soil particles and pore water which destroys sediment or soil stratigraphy, changes rates of chemical reactions and sediment/soil-water exchange, and modifies sediment/soil physical properties such as grain size, porosity, and permeability.

narrower.label: root respiration
narrower.definition: The oxidation of organic compounds by plant roots, accompanied by oxygen absorption and carbon dioxide release.

definitions.text: The oxidation of organic compounds by plant roots, accompanied by oxygen absorption and carbon dioxide release.

narrower.label: seedling emergence
narrower.definition: Seedling emergence describes the first emergence of the seed planted under the ground.

narrower.definition: Exchange of ions associated with charged soil-mineral surfaces with ions in the soil solution.

narrower.label: soil adsorption
narrower.definition: The process by which ions or molecules attach to the surfaces of soil solids.

definitions.text: The process by which ions or molecules attach to the surfaces of soil solids.

narrower.label: soil polymer adsorption
narrower.definition: The transfer of a polymer molecule from the solution phase to an adsorbed state on a soil clay-particle surface, with interaction between the soil particle and the polymer molecule.

definitions.text: The transfer of a polymer molecule from the solution phase to an adsorbed state on a soil clay-particle surface, with interaction between the soil particle and the polymer molecule.

narrower.label: soil water adsorption
narrower.definition: Attachment of water molecules to clay surfaces, where they may be held by hydrogen bonding or electrostatic attraction; the water so held is termed adsorbed water.

definitions.text: Attachment of water molecules to clay surfaces, where they may be held by hydrogen bonding or electrostatic attraction; the water so held is termed adsorbed water.

narrower.label: soil anion exclusion
narrower.definition: A process opposite to adsorption in which the concentration in the soil solution is higher than in the solid phase.

definitions.text: A process opposite to adsorption in which the concentration in the soil solution is higher than in the solid phase.

narrower.label: soil acidification
narrower.definition: The lowering of the soil pH of the build-up of hydrogen and aluminium ions in the soil and the leaching of base cations such as calcium, magnesium, potassium and sodium. Soil acidification negatively affects soil fertility and compromises the production capacity of most agricultural soils.

narrower.label: soil crust formation
narrower.definition: The process in which soil aggregates disperse, followed by particle orientation and hardening through desiccation to form a crust.

definitions.text: The process in which soil aggregates disperse, followed by particle orientation and hardening through desiccation to form a crust.

narrower.label: soil crusting
narrower.definition: The formation of a thin soil-surface crust through disruption of aggregates at the soil-air interface, followed by dispersion, particle reorientation, and drying or desiccation.

definitions.text: The formation of a thin soil-surface crust through disruption of aggregates at the soil-air interface, followed by dispersion, particle reorientation, and drying or desiccation.

narrower.label: soil degradation
narrower.definition: Soil degradation refers to the diminishing capacity of the  soil to provide ecosystem goods and services as desired by its stakeholders.

definitions.text: Soil degradation refers to the diminishing capacity of the  soil to provide ecosystem goods and services as desired by its stakeholders.
A decline in soil quality such that the soil cannot perform one or several of its principal functions.

narrower.label: soil compaction
narrower.definition: The increase in density and a decline of macro-porosity in a soil that impairs the functions of both the top- and subsoil, and impedes roots penetration and water gaseous exchanges.

definitions.text: The increase in density and a decline of macro-porosity in a soil that impairs the functions of both the top- and subsoil, and impedes roots penetration and water gaseous exchanges.

Compression and deformation of an unsaturated soil mass into a smaller volume, decreasing total porosity and macroporosity; the volume decrease occurs primarily through expulsion or compression of soil air.

narrower.label: soil salinization
narrower.definition: Soil salinization is defined as the increase in water-soluble salts in soil which is responsible for increasing the osmotic pressure of the  soil.  In turn,  this negatively affects plant growth because less water is made available to plants.

narrower.label: soil sealing
narrower.definition: Permanent covering of the soil surface with impermeable artificial materials, leading to non-reversible loss of soil and most of its ecosystem services

definitions.text: Permanent covering of the soil surface with impermeable artificial materials, leading to non-reversible loss of soil and most of its ecosystem services

narrower.label: soil sealing consistence
narrower.definition: The sealing consistence of soil describes the resistance of the soil to the formation of a surface crust or compacted layer, which can impede water infiltration and root penetration. This phenomenon typically occurs in fine-textured soils, such as clays and silts, where the particles are tightly bound, leading to a hardened surface layer upon wetting and drying. Sealing consistence affects water movement and can lead to surface runoff and erosion in agricultural soils. Source: Soil Science Society of America (SSSA). (2008). Glossary of Soil Science Terms. Soil Science Society of America.

narrower.label: soil sealing thickness
narrower.definition: The sealing thickness refers to the depth of the compacted or sealed layer within the soil, which is typically a result of intense rainfall, drying, or tillage practices. This layer, which forms in fine-textured soils, can significantly reduce water infiltration and root growth, leading to reduced soil aeration and potential surface runoff. The sealing thickness property is crucial for understanding soil erosion risks and water management in agricultural systems. Source: Pagliai, M., & Vignozzi, N. (2002). Soil Structure and Soil Quality: A Review of the State of the Art. Agriculture, Ecosystems & Environment, 88(3), 77-86.

narrower.definition: A managed salt-removal process in which water equal to the leaching requirement is applied to a field and allowed to flow through and beyond the root zone to remove excess salts.

narrower.definition: Uptake of water by soil colloids, described as hydration at exchange sites and exchangeable cations, followed by growth of water films and capillary condensation as relative vapor pressure rises.

narrower.definition: Frost heaving (or a frost heave) is an upwards swelling of soil during freezing conditions caused by an increasing presence of ice as it grows towards the surface, upwards from the depth in the soil where freezing temperatures have penetrated into the soil (the freezing front or freezing boundary).

narrower.definition: Soil salinization is defined as the increase in water-soluble salts in soil which is responsible for increasing the osmotic pressure of the  soil.  In turn,  this negatively affects plant growth because less water is made available to plants.

narrower.label: soil sealing consistence
narrower.definition: The sealing consistence of soil describes the resistance of the soil to the formation of a surface crust or compacted layer, which can impede water infiltration and root penetration. This phenomenon typically occurs in fine-textured soils, such as clays and silts, where the particles are tightly bound, leading to a hardened surface layer upon wetting and drying. Sealing consistence affects water movement and can lead to surface runoff and erosion in agricultural soils. Source: Soil Science Society of America (SSSA). (2008). Glossary of Soil Science Terms. Soil Science Society of America.

narrower.label: soil sealing thickness
narrower.definition: The sealing thickness refers to the depth of the compacted or sealed layer within the soil, which is typically a result of intense rainfall, drying, or tillage practices. This layer, which forms in fine-textured soils, can significantly reduce water infiltration and root growth, leading to reduced soil aeration and potential surface runoff. The sealing thickness property is crucial for understanding soil erosion risks and water management in agricultural systems. Source: Pagliai, M., & Vignozzi, N. (2002). Soil Structure and Soil Quality: A Review of the State of the Art. Agriculture, Ecosystems & Environment, 88(3), 77-86.

narrower.definition: Soil Erosion Activity Period refers to the time frame during which soil erosion processes, such as wind or water erosion, are most active in a given area. This period is influenced by climatic conditions, seasonal rainfall, and land use, and it helps in assessing the vulnerability of soils to degradation. Source: USDA NRCS, 'Soil Erosion and Conservation'

narrower.label: soil erosion category
narrower.definition: Soil Erosion Category classifies the type and severity of erosion in a given area. Categories are often based on the nature of the erosive forces (e.g., water, wind) and the degree of soil loss, ranging from slight to severe. This classification aids in prioritizing conservation efforts and understanding the potential impacts on soil quality. Source: FAO, 'Soil Erosion and Conservation'

narrower.definition: Sheet erosion, which is a uniform removal of soil in thin layers from sloping land, occurs where the velocity of surface run-off is about 0.3 to 0.6 meters per second.

narrower.label: soil surface age
narrower.definition: Surface Age refers to the estimated age of a surface layer of soil or landform, which is important for understanding the degree of soil weathering, development, and fertility. Older surfaces may have more developed soils, while younger surfaces may be less fertile and more prone to erosion. Source: FAO, 'Soil Formation and Evolution'

narrower.label: soil biological properties
narrower.definition: This concerns soil properties related to the microbial and faunal activity in soil. These organisms include earthworms, nematodes, protozoa, fungi, bacteria and different arthropods. Soil biology plays a vital role in determining many soil characteristics, yet, being a relatively new science, much remains unknown about soil biology and about how the nature of soil is affected.

definitions.text: This concerns soil properties related to the microbial and faunal activity in soil. These organisms include earthworms, nematodes, protozoa, fungi, bacteria and different arthropods. Soil biology plays a vital role in determining many soil characteristics, yet, being a relatively new science, much remains unknown about soil biology and about how the nature of soil is affected.

Soil biological properties refer to the biological components in the soil, including microbial life such as bacterial and fungal colonies, which are affected by changes in soil chemical and physical properties, such as acidity and organic matter content. These properties can be assessed through indicators like enzyme activities, which vary with management practices and land use.

narrower.label: biological abundance
narrower.definition: The Biological Abundance evaluates the presence and quantity of soil organisms, such as microbes, insects, and earthworms. This property reflects soil health, nutrient cycling, and organic matter decomposition, which are vital for maintaining soil fertility. Source: Lavelle, P., & Spain, A.V. (2001). Soil Ecology.

narrower.definition: Content or amount of total nitrogen in soil.

definitions.text: Content or amount of total nitrogen in soil.

Total nitrogen encompasses all nitrogen forms in soil, including organic nitrogen in humus and inorganic nitrogen such as ammonium (NH₄⁺) and nitrate (NO₃⁻). Nitrogen is essential for plant growth, being a vital component of amino acids, proteins, and chlorophyll. Total nitrogen is a key indicator of soil fertility and its capacity to sustain long-term crop productivity. Source: Brady & Weil (2017).

narrower.label: soil chemical properties
narrower.definition: Chemical properties of soils include the following aspects: inorganic matters of soil, organic matters in soil, colloidal properties of soil particles and soil reactions and buffering action in acidic soils and basic soils.

definitions.text: Chemical properties of soils include the following aspects: inorganic matters of soil, organic matters in soil, colloidal properties of soil particles and soil reactions and buffering action in acidic soils and basic soils.

Soil chemical properties refer to the chemical attributes of soil that influence its ability to supply nutrients to plants, retain harmful elements, and affect plant growth and microbial populations. These properties include nutrient concentrations, pH levels, and the presence of elements such as nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium, which are critical for soil quality assessment and agricultural productivity.

narrower.label: base saturation
narrower.definition: The ratio of the quantity of exchangeable bases to the cation exchange capacity.

definitions.text: The ratio of the quantity of exchangeable bases to the cation exchange capacity.

Base saturation represents the percentage of the soil's cation exchange capacity (CEC) occupied by basic cations such as calcium (Ca²⁺), magnesium (Mg²⁺), potassium (K⁺), and sodium (Na⁺). Higher base saturation typically correlates with higher fertility and a greater ability to supply essential nutrients to plants. This parameter also influences soil pH buffering capacity. Source: Brady & Weil (2017).

definitions.text: Content or amount of total nitrogen in soil.

Total nitrogen encompasses all nitrogen forms in soil, including organic nitrogen in humus and inorganic nitrogen such as ammonium (NH₄⁺) and nitrate (NO₃⁻). Nitrogen is essential for plant growth, being a vital component of amino acids, proteins, and chlorophyll. Total nitrogen is a key indicator of soil fertility and its capacity to sustain long-term crop productivity. Source: Brady & Weil (2017).
