narrower.label: Umbrisols
narrower.definition: Umbrisols have a significant accumulation of organic matter in the mineral surface soil and a low base saturation somewhere within the first metre (in most cases in the mineral surface soil). Umbrisols are the logical counterpart of soils with a chernic or mollic horizon and a high base saturation throughout (Chernozems, Kastanozems and Phaeozems). Many of these soils are classified in other systems as several Great Groups of Entisols and Inceptisols (United States of America), Sombric Brunisols and Humic Regosols (France), Mountain-meadow soils (former USSR) and Mucky-dark-humus soils (Russia), Brown podzolic soils (e.g. Indonesia) and Umbrisols (Romania). In the Soil Map of the World (FAO–UNESCO, 1971–1981) most of them belong to Humic Cambisols and Umbric Regosols.

narrower.label: Vertisols
narrower.definition: Vertisols are heavy clay soils with a high proportion of swelling clays. These soils form deep wide cracks from the surface downward when they dry out, which happens in most years. Common local names for Vertisols are Black cotton soils and Regur (India), Black turf soils (South Africa) or Margalites (Indonesia). In national soil classification systems they are called Slitozems or Dark vertic soils (Russia), Vertosols (Australia), Vertissolos (Brazil) and Vertisols (United States of America).

narrower.definition: The Voids Classification categorizes voids or pores in the soil based on size, shape, and arrangement. These voids are critical for water movement, air circulation, and root penetration. They are classified into macropores (large), mesopores (medium), and micropores (small). Source: Hillel, D. (2004). Introduction to Environmental Soil Physics.

Shallow groundwater can influence soil salinity and nutrient availability, while deep groundwater may limit water access for plants. Source: USDA NRCS, 'Groundwater and Soil'

narrower.definition: The proportionality coefficient relating water flux density through soil to the hydraulic gradient; its value characterizes both the soil medium and the water and depends on the saturation or moisture state.

Hydraulic conductivity refers to the rate at which water moves through soil pores under a unit hydraulic gradient. It reflects the soil's ability to transmit water, influenced by texture, structure, and porosity. Soils with high hydraulic conductivity, like sandy soils, allow rapid water movement, while clayey soils exhibit slower water flow. This property is critical for understanding water infiltration, drainage, and irrigation management. Source: Brady, N.C., & Weil, R.R. (2017). The Nature and Properties of Soils.

narrower.definition: The amount of water removed from soil by heating at 105°C to constant weight, expressed as a fraction or percentage on a mass or volume basis. On a gravimetric basis it equals the difference between wet and dry soil mass divided by dry soil mass.

definitions.text: The amount of water removed from soil by heating at 105°C to constant weight, expressed as a fraction or percentage on a mass or volume basis. On a gravimetric basis it equals the difference between wet and dry soil mass divided by dry soil mass.

Soil-water content is the basic state characteristic of soil; it expresses the relative quantity of water in the soil. Soil-water content can be expressed as the ratio of water amount and the amount of soil.

The Moisture Content measures the amount of water present in soil, expressed as a percentage of its dry weight. This property is critical for assessing soil water retention, irrigation needs, and plant-available water. Source: Hillel, D. (2004). Introduction to Environmental Soil Physics.

narrower.definition: The maximum rate at which water can infiltrate into the soil profile.

narrower.label: soil water potential
narrower.definition: Total soil water potential is defined as the amount of work per unit quantity of pure water that must be done by external forces to transfer reversibly and isothermally an infinitesimal amount of water from the standard state to the soil at the point under consideration.

definitions.text: Total soil water potential is defined as the amount of work per unit quantity of pure water that must be done by external forces to transfer reversibly and isothermally an infinitesimal amount of water from the standard state to the soil at the point under consideration.

The amount of work that a unit quantity of water in an equilibrium soil-moisture system can do when it moves to a reference pool of pure water at atmospheric pressure, at the same temperature and level as the soil moisture.

narrower.label: soil matric potential
narrower.definition: The negative potential of water in unsaturated soil arising from soil solids, curvature at interfaces due to surface tension, and cohesion and adhesion within the soil matrix; also called capillary potential.

definitions.text: The negative potential of water in unsaturated soil arising from soil solids, curvature at interfaces due to surface tension, and cohesion and adhesion within the soil matrix; also called capillary potential.

narrower.label: soil water regimes
narrower.definition: The presence or absence either of ground water or of plant available water (i.e., water held at a tension of less than 1500 kPa) in the soil or in specific horizons during periods of the year. A generally accepted classification of soil moisture regimes from wet to dry includes aquic, udic, ustic, aridic, and xeric.

narrower.label: stickiness
narrower.definition: The Stickiness measures the soil’s tendency to adhere to surfaces or objects when wet. It is influenced by clay content and organic matter and affects soil workability and machinery use. Source: Hillel, D. (2004). Introduction to Environmental Soil Physics.

narrower.label: soil sorption
narrower.definition: Selective process, which occurs on soil particles smaller than 0.002mm (<2µm); these small particles have colloidal properties, are able to hold and exchange ions, water or gases.

narrower.definition: The resistance that must be overcome to produce a specified deformation of soil.

narrower.definition: The way individual particles of sand, silt and clay are assembled to form aggregates; described in terms of grade (degree of aggregation), class (average size), type of aggregates (form) and the nature and distribution of pores and pore spaces.

narrower.definition: A naturally occurring cluster of soil particles whose internal binding forces are much stronger than the forces between adjacent aggregates.

narrower.definition: A pore between soil aggregates that results from the arrangement of structural elements and the characteristics of the aggregates; also called a structural pore.

narrower.label: pore abundance
narrower.definition: The Pores Abundance describes the quantity of soil pores, ranging from few to many. It influences water infiltration, root growth, and soil aeration. Pore abundance is crucial for assessing soil health and productivity. Source: Soil Survey Manual (USDA, 2017).

narrower.label: soil crack depth
narrower.definition: The Soil Crack Depth refers to the measurement of the vertical depth of cracks formed in soil, which is typically observed in dry conditions when the soil shrinks. Cracks are more common in clayey soils that experience significant shrinkage upon drying. The depth of these cracks can indicate soil moisture levels, compaction, and the ability of the soil to expand and contract, which affects water infiltration and root penetration. Source: McSweeney, K. (2009). Soil and Water Conservation Handbook. CRC Press.

narrower.label: soil crack distance
narrower.definition: The Soil Crack Distance refers to the horizontal spacing between cracks in the soil surface, which can occur due to the shrinkage of soil as it dries. Cracks form when water content decreases, and their distance is an indicator of the soil's shrink-swell behavior. Larger distances between cracks generally indicate more severe soil shrinkage, which can affect root growth and water infiltration. Source: McSweeney, K. (2009). Soil and Water Conservation Handbook. CRC Press.

narrower.label: soil crack width
narrower.definition: The Soil Crack Width refers to the measurement of the gap or space between the sides of soil cracks. The width of these cracks is typically influenced by soil moisture content and texture. Wider cracks are indicative of drier conditions and are commonly found in soils with high clay content, which tend to shrink and form deep cracks when the moisture content is reduced. Source: McSweeney, K. (2009). Soil and Water Conservation Handbook. CRC Press.

Soils can be classified into textures such as sandy, loamy, or clayey, each with distinct characteristics affecting soil management. Source: Soil Science Society of America. (2008). Total carbon in soil includes both organic carbon (from plant and microbial residues) and inorganic carbon (primarily carbonates). It is a fundamental component of soil organic matter, influencing soil fertility, structure, and water retention. High carbon levels are associated with better soil health and productivity. Source: USDA NRCS.

Inorganic carbon in soil primarily consists of carbonates like calcium carbonate and magnesium carbonate. It contributes to soil pH buffering and is a significant feature of arid and calcareous soils. Excess inorganic carbon can immobilize certain nutrients, requiring careful management in agricultural systems. Source: Soil Science Society of America.

narrower.label: soil organic carbon
narrower.definition: Soil organic carbon (SOC) refers to the carbon held within the soil and is expressed as a percentage by weight (gC/Kg soil). Climatic shifts in temperature and precipitation have a major influence on the decomposition and amount of SOC stored within an ecosystem and that released into the atmosphere. Globally, the amount of carbon stored in soils is twice the amount that is stored in all terrestrial plants. Soil organic carbon (SOC) is essential for maintaining fertility, water retention, and plant production in terrestrial ecosystems. The amount of SOC stored within an ecosystem, is dependent on the quantity and quality of organic matter returned to the soil matrix, the soils ability to retain organic carbon (a function of texture and caption exchange capacity), and biotic influences of both temperature and precipitation. The global decline in SOC as a result of deforestation, shifting cultivation and arable cropping have made significant contributions to increased levels of atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO2).

Organic carbon refers to the carbon component of soil organic matter, derived from decomposed plant and microbial residues. It serves as a key energy source for soil microbes and influences nutrient cycling, soil structure, and water retention. Organic carbon is a primary indicator of soil fertility and health. Source: IPCC, 'Guidelines for National Greenhouse Gas Inventories'

narrower.label: soil field moisture capacity
narrower.definition: The soil moisture content reached after a soil has been thoroughly wetted and allowed to drain freely under gravity without loss by evaporation, with transmission pores drained and their water replaced by air.

narrower.label: soil water potential
narrower.definition: Total soil water potential is defined as the amount of work per unit quantity of pure water that must be done by external forces to transfer reversibly and isothermally an infinitesimal amount of water from the standard state to the soil at the point under consideration.

definitions.text: Total soil water potential is defined as the amount of work per unit quantity of pure water that must be done by external forces to transfer reversibly and isothermally an infinitesimal amount of water from the standard state to the soil at the point under consideration.

A generally accepted classification of soil moisture regimes from wet to dry includes aquic, udic, ustic, aridic, and xeric.

narrower.label: soil pH
narrower.definition: Soil pH is a measure of the acidity or alkalinity of the soil. A pH value is actually a measure of hydrogen ion concentration. It is a ‘reverse’ scale in that a very acid soil has a low pH and a high hydrogen ion concentration.

definitions.text: Soil pH is a measure of the acidity or alkalinity of the soil. A pH value is actually a measure of hydrogen ion concentration. It is a ‘reverse’ scale in that a very acid soil has a low pH and a high hydrogen ion concentration.

Soil pH measures the concentration of hydrogen ions (H⁺) in the soil solution, indicating its acidity or alkalinity on a scale from 1 to 14. Neutral soils have a pH of 7, while values below 7 are acidic and above are alkaline. Soil pH significantly affects nutrient availability, microbial activity, and plant growth. For instance, nutrients like phosphorus are most available in a pH range of 6 to 7. Lime or sulfur applications can adjust soil pH to optimize conditions for crops. Source: USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service (NRCS).

narrower.definition: Soil depth defines the root space and the volume of soil from where the plants fulfil their water and nutrient demands.

definitions.text: Soil depth defines the root space and the volume of soil from where the plants fulfil their water and nutrient demands.

The Soil Depth measures the vertical distance from the soil surface to an impenetrable layer, such as bedrock or a hardpan. Soil depth is a crucial factor influencing root development, water storage, and plant growth. Shallow soils may limit root growth, while deep soils can support more extensive root systems. Source: Brady, N. C., & Weil, R. R. (2008). The Nature and Properties of Soils (14th ed.). Pearson Prentice Hall.

narrower.label: soil depth bedrock
narrower.definition: The Soil Depth Bedrock refers to the distance from the soil surface to the underlying bedrock layer. This measurement is important for understanding the soil's capacity to support plant growth, as soils with shallow bedrock tend to have limited rooting depth, affecting water retention and nutrient availability. Source: FAO (2006). Guidelines for Soil Description (4th ed.). Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations.

narrower.label: Modified Universal Soil Loss Equation
narrower.definition: MUSLE is a modification of the Universal Soil Loss Equation (USLE). MUSLE is similar to USLE except for the energy component. USLE depends strictly upon rainfall as the source of erosive energy. MUSLE uses storm-based runoff volumes and runoff peak flows to simulate erosion and sediment yield (Williams 1995). The use of runoff variables rather than rainfall erosivity as the driving force enables MUSLE to estimate sediment yields for individual storm events.

narrower.label: salt cover
narrower.definition: Salt cover refers to the accumulation of salts on the surface of the soil, often visible as a crystalline crust. This phenomenon occurs when capillary action causes soluble salts to move upwards through the soil, where they crystallize as water evaporates. Salt cover can interfere with seed germination, plant growth, and water infiltration, and is commonly found in arid and semi-arid regions with high evaporation rates. Source: Brady, N.C., & Weil, R.R. (2008). The Nature and Properties of Soils (14th ed.). Pearson Education.

narrower.label: salt presence
narrower.definition: The salt presence of soil refers to the concentration of soluble salts, such as sodium, calcium, and magnesium, within the soil profile. High salt levels can lead to soil salinity, negatively affecting plant growth by altering water availability and soil structure. The presence of salts is typically measured using electrical conductivity (EC) or specific ion concentration tests. Soils with high salt presence are often found in arid regions where evaporation exceeds precipitation, leading to salt accumulation at or near the surface. Source: Rhoades, J.D., & Kandiah, A. (1992). Soil Salinity Management in Agriculture. Springer.

narrower.label: salt thickness
narrower.definition: Salt thickness refers to the depth of the soil profile at which soluble salts are present in significant concentrations. This property is particularly important in regions subject to evaporation and capillary rise, where salts accumulate near the surface or at specific depths. Salt thickness can impact soil fertility and water retention, as the concentrated salts can inhibit root growth and water uptake. This property is commonly determined through soil sampling and electrical conductivity measurements at various depths. Source: United States Salinity Laboratory Staff. (1954). Diagnosis and Improvement of Saline and Alkali Soils. U.S. Department of Agriculture Handbook No. 60.

narrower.label: soil air
narrower.definition: Soil air is the gaseous phase of the soil. Soil pores are filled with air and water, and there is a dynamic equilibrium between water and air content within a soil. The main constituents of soil air, as in the atmosphere, are nitrogen, oxygen, and carbon dioxide.

narrower.label: soil organic carbon
narrower.definition: Soil organic carbon (SOC) refers to the carbon held within the soil and is expressed as a percentage by weight (gC/Kg soil). Climatic shifts in temperature and precipitation have a major influence on the decomposition and amount of SOC stored within an ecosystem and that released into the atmosphere. Globally, the amount of carbon stored in soils is twice the amount that is stored in all terrestrial plants. Soil organic carbon (SOC) is essential for maintaining fertility, water retention, and plant production in terrestrial ecosystems. The amount of SOC stored within an ecosystem, is dependent on the quantity and quality of organic matter returned to the soil matrix, the soils ability to retain organic carbon (a function of texture and caption exchange capacity), and biotic influences of both temperature and precipitation. The global decline in SOC as a result of deforestation, shifting cultivation and arable cropping have made significant contributions to increased levels of atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO2).

narrower.label: bleached sand
narrower.definition: The Bleached Sand refers to the physical characteristic of sandy soil that has undergone a bleaching process due to leaching, where minerals such as iron and other elements have been removed by water. This process often occurs in areas with high rainfall, leading to a soil that appears lighter in color. Bleached sand typically indicates low fertility and poor nutrient-holding capacity due to the lack of iron and other nutrients that are washed away. Source: Brady, N. C., & Weil, R. R. (2008). The Nature and Properties of Soils (14th ed.). Pearson Prentice Hall.

narrower.label: soil organic carbon
narrower.definition: Soil organic carbon (SOC) refers to the carbon held within the soil and is expressed as a percentage by weight (gC/Kg soil). Climatic shifts in temperature and precipitation have a major influence on the decomposition and amount of SOC stored within an ecosystem and that released into the atmosphere. Globally, the amount of carbon stored in soils is twice the amount that is stored in all terrestrial plants. Soil organic carbon (SOC) is essential for maintaining fertility, water retention, and plant production in terrestrial ecosystems. The amount of SOC stored within an ecosystem, is dependent on the quantity and quality of organic matter returned to the soil matrix, the soils ability to retain organic carbon (a function of texture and caption exchange capacity), and biotic influences of both temperature and precipitation. The global decline in SOC as a result of deforestation, shifting cultivation and arable cropping have made significant contributions to increased levels of atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO2).

Organic carbon refers to the carbon component of soil organic matter, derived from decomposed plant and microbial residues. It serves as a key energy source for soil microbes and influences nutrient cycling, soil structure, and water retention. Organic carbon is a primary indicator of soil fertility and health. Source: Brady & Weil (2017).

narrower.definition: Soil Carbon Density measures the amount of organic carbon stored in a given volume of soil, typically expressed in tons per hectare. Source: IPCC, 'Guidelines for National Greenhouse Gas Inventories'

narrower.label: macronutrients
narrower.definition: The major source of energy and bulk (volume) in our diets, macronutrients are needed in large quantities (in gram range). They include carbohydrates, proteins and fats. They are a main source of dietary energy, which is measured in calories. Obtaining sufficient energy is essential for everyone in order to maintain body growth, development and good health. Adequate potassium levels improve crop yield, quality, and resistance to stress. Source: Soil Science Society of America.

narrower.definition: Total iron includes all iron forms in the soil, from soluble ferrous iron (Fe²⁺) to insoluble ferric iron (Fe³⁺). Deficiency, often seen in alkaline soils, results in chlorosis, while excessive iron can cause toxicity in acidic soils. Source: Soil Chemistry by Bohn et al.

narrower.definition: Soil-borne wheat mosaic virus (SBWMV) is a rod-shaped plant pathogen that can cause severe stunting and mosaic in susceptible wheat, barley and rye cultivars.

narrower.label: termites
narrower.definition: Termites are social insects that build large nests in soil or wood and can occasionally cause damage to wooden structures. They are sometimes called 'white ants', however they belong to a completely different insect group (Order Isoptera) to true ants (Order Hymenoptera).

narrower.label: soil microorganisms
narrower.definition: Microorganisms in soil are important because they affect soil structure and fertility. Soil microorganisms can be classified as bacteria, actinomycetes, fungi, algae and protozoa. Each of these groups has characteristics that define them and their functions in soil

narrower.definition: Phylogenetically diverse, predominantly microscopic free-living, symbiotic organisms capable of oxygenic photosynthesis. Traditionally, soil algae include photoautotrophic prokaryotes (cyanobacteria, blue-green algae) and photoautotrophic protists (eukaryotic algae).

narrower.label: soil pores
narrower.definition: Voids or spaces between the solid components of soil, which may be occupied by water or air.

definitions.text: Voids or spaces between the solid components of soil, which may be occupied by water or air.

narrower.label: interaggregate pores
narrower.definition: A pore between soil aggregates that results from the arrangement of structural elements and the characteristics of the aggregates; also called a structural pore.

definitions.text: A pore between soil aggregates that results from the arrangement of structural elements and the characteristics of the aggregates; also called a structural pore.

narrower.label: interstructural pores
narrower.definition: A soil pore delimited by structural units, generally forming a planar crevice between those units.

definitions.text: A soil pore delimited by structural units, generally forming a planar crevice between those units.

narrower.label: intraaggregate pores
narrower.definition: A pore within a soil aggregate whose characteristics are determined by soil texture and the packing of elementary particles; also called a textural pore.

definitions.text: A pore within a soil aggregate whose characteristics are determined by soil texture and the packing of elementary particles; also called a textural pore.

narrower.label: matrix pores
narrower.definition: A generally small textural pore formed by the packing of primary soil particles.

definitions.text: A generally small textural pore formed by the packing of primary soil particles.

narrower.label: non matrix pores
narrower.definition: A large soil void created by roots, burrowing animals, compressed air, or other agents.

definitions.text: A large soil void created by roots, burrowing animals, compressed air, or other agents.

narrower.label: pore abundance
narrower.definition: The Pores Abundance describes the quantity of soil pores, ranging from few to many. It influences water infiltration, root growth, and soil aeration. Pore abundance is crucial for assessing soil health and productivity. Source: Soil Survey Manual (USDA, 2017).

narrower.label: soil macropore
narrower.definition: A soil pore that serves as a preferential water-flow path, identified by its flow behavior and continuity.

definitions.text: A soil pore that serves as a preferential water-flow path, identified by its flow behavior and continuity.

narrower.label: soil biopore
narrower.definition: A soil pore formed through interactions between soil and its biota, such as a root channel, wormhole, or animal burrow.

definitions.text: A soil pore formed through interactions between soil and its biota, such as a root channel, wormhole, or animal burrow.

narrower.label: soil cracks
narrower.definition: Openings in soil that can form through shrinkage of clayey soil, chemical weathering of bedrock, cultivation, or freeze-thaw cycling.

definitions.text: Openings in soil that can form through shrinkage of clayey soil, chemical weathering of bedrock, cultivation, or freeze-thaw cycling.

narrower.label: soil crack depth
narrower.definition: The Soil Crack Depth refers to the measurement of the vertical depth of cracks formed in soil, which is typically observed in dry conditions when the soil shrinks. Cracks are more common in clayey soils that experience significant shrinkage upon drying. The depth of these cracks can indicate soil moisture levels, compaction, and the ability of the soil to expand and contract, which affects water infiltration and root penetration. Source: McSweeney, K. (2009). Soil and Water Conservation Handbook. CRC Press.

narrower.label: soil crack distance
narrower.definition: The Soil Crack Distance refers to the horizontal spacing between cracks in the soil surface, which can occur due to the shrinkage of soil as it dries. Cracks form when water content decreases, and their distance is an indicator of the soil's shrink-swell behavior. Larger distances between cracks generally indicate more severe soil shrinkage, which can affect root growth and water infiltration. Source: McSweeney, K. (2009). Soil and Water Conservation Handbook. CRC Press.

narrower.label: soil crack width
narrower.definition: The Soil Crack Width refers to the measurement of the gap or space between the sides of soil cracks. The width of these cracks is typically influenced by soil moisture content and texture. Wider cracks are indicative of drier conditions and are commonly found in soils with high clay content, which tend to shrink and form deep cracks when the moisture content is reduced. Source: McSweeney, K. (2009). Soil and Water Conservation Handbook. CRC Press.

narrower.label: soil mesopore
narrower.definition: A soil pore with an equivalent cylindrical diameter between 0.2 and 30 µm in the size classification recommended in this text.

narrower.label: soil micropore
narrower.definition: A soil pore with an equivalent cylindrical diameter less than 0.2 µm in the size classification recommended in this text.

narrower.label: soil pore size
narrower.definition: The dimension used to characterize soil pores by diameter, including equivalent cylindrical diameter in soil-pore size classifications.

The Pores Size categorizes soil pores by their diameter, such as macro-pores, meso-pores, and micro-pores. This property determines water retention, air movement, and root penetration in soil. Source: Brady, N.C., & Weil, R.R. (2008). The Nature and Properties of Soils.

narrower.label: soil preferential flow path
narrower.definition: A distinct conducting pathway that occupies a small fraction of the total soil pore space and carries preferential water flow through the soil profile rather than through the whole pore network.

narrower.label: textural pores
narrower.definition: Pores within an aggregate, determined by textural characteristics and the packing state of elementary particles; also called intraaggregate pores.

narrower.label: soil surface seal
narrower.definition: A thin, dense layer at the soil surface characterized by low porosity, high density, and low permeability to air and water.

definitions.text: A thin, dense layer at the soil surface characterized by low porosity, high density, and low permeability to air and water.

top_concepts.label: soil threats
top_concepts.definition: Soil threats are processes that could degrade (some of) the functions of soils and the services that soils provide. Examples of soil threats are: acidification, compaction, contamination (pollution), decline in soil organic matter, decline in soil biodiversity, desertification, erosion, flooding and water logging, landslides, salinization.

narrower.label: soil acidification
narrower.definition: The lowering of the soil pH of the build-up of hydrogen and aluminium ions in the soil and the leaching of base cations such as calcium, magnesium, potassium and sodium. Soil acidification negatively affects soil fertility and compromises the production capacity of most agricultural soils.

narrower.label: soil compaction
narrower.definition: The increase in density and a decline of macro-porosity in a soil that impairs the functions of both the top- and subsoil, and impedes roots penetration and water gaseous exchanges.

definitions.text: The increase in density and a decline of macro-porosity in a soil that impairs the functions of both the top- and subsoil, and impedes roots penetration and water gaseous exchanges.

Compression and deformation of an unsaturated soil mass into a smaller volume, decreasing total porosity and macroporosity; the volume decrease occurs primarily through expulsion or compression of soil air.

narrower.label: soil degradation
narrower.definition: Soil degradation refers to the diminishing capacity of the  soil to provide ecosystem goods and services as desired by its stakeholders.

definitions.text: Soil degradation refers to the diminishing capacity of the  soil to provide ecosystem goods and services as desired by its stakeholders.
A decline in soil quality such that the soil cannot perform one or several of its principal functions.

narrower.label: soil salinization
narrower.definition: Soil salinization is defined as the increase in water-soluble salts in soil which is responsible for increasing the osmotic pressure of the  soil.  In turn,  this negatively affects plant growth because less water is made available to plants.

narrower.label: soil sealing
narrower.definition: Permanent covering of the soil surface with impermeable artificial materials, leading to non-reversible loss of soil and most of its ecosystem services

narrower.label: soil sealing consistence
narrower.definition: The sealing consistence of soil describes the resistance of the soil to the formation of a surface crust or compacted layer, which can impede water infiltration and root penetration. This phenomenon typically occurs in fine-textured soils, such as clays and silts, where the particles are tightly bound, leading to a hardened surface layer upon wetting and drying. Sealing consistence affects water movement and can lead to surface runoff and erosion in agricultural soils. Source: Soil Science Society of America (SSSA). (2008). Glossary of Soil Science Terms. Soil Science Society of America.

narrower.label: soil sealing thickness
narrower.definition: The sealing thickness refers to the depth of the compacted or sealed layer within the soil, which is typically a result of intense rainfall, drying, or tillage practices. This layer, which forms in fine-textured soils, can significantly reduce water infiltration and root growth, leading to reduced soil aeration and potential surface runoff. The sealing thickness property is crucial for understanding soil erosion risks and water management in agricultural systems. Source: Pagliai, M., & Vignozzi, N. (2002). Soil Structure and Soil Quality: A Review of the State of the Art. Agriculture, Ecosystems & Environment, 88(3), 77-86.

narrower.label: accelerated erosion
narrower.definition: Erosion much more rapid than normal erosion, natural erosion, or geologic erosion, and occurring primarily as a result of the influence of the activities of man or, in some cases, of other animals or natural catastrophes that expose bare surfaces (for example, fires).

narrower.label: harvesting erosion
narrower.definition: Harvesting erosion is offsite losses of soil adhering to the crop during harvest, mainly of root and tuber crops.

definitions.text: Harvesting erosion is offsite losses of soil adhering to the crop during harvest, mainly of root and tuber crops.

narrower.label: livestock trampling erosion
narrower.definition: Erosion caused by livestock trampling is onsite soil loss occurring after soil compaction, overgrazing and removal or reduction of vegetation cover.

definitions.text: Erosion caused by livestock trampling is onsite soil loss occurring after soil compaction, overgrazing and removal or reduction of vegetation cover.

narrower.definition: Soil erosion as released by tillage activities.

narrower.label: soil erosion activity period
narrower.definition: Soil Erosion Activity Period refers to the time frame during which soil erosion processes, such as wind or water erosion, are most active in a given area. This period is influenced by climatic conditions, seasonal rainfall, and land use, and it helps in assessing the vulnerability of soils to degradation. Source: USDA NRCS, 'Soil Erosion and Conservation'

narrower.definition: Soil Erosion Area Affected refers to the extent of land area that has been impacted by soil erosion processes, such as water or wind erosion. This property is important for evaluating the severity of soil degradation in a given region and helps in identifying areas that require soil conservation measures. Source: USDA NRCS, 'Soil Erosion Research and Technology Transfer'

narrower.label: soil erosion category
narrower.definition: Soil Erosion Category classifies the type and severity of erosion in a given area. Categories are often based on the nature of the erosive forces (e.g., water, wind) and the degree of soil loss, ranging from slight to severe. This classification aids in prioritizing conservation efforts and understanding the potential impacts on soil quality. Source: FAO, 'Soil Erosion and Conservation'

The degree of erosion helps in assessing the extent of soil degradation and informs decisions on soil conservation and land management. Source: FAO, 'Soil Erosion and Conservation'

narrower.label: gully erosion
narrower.definition: Gully erosion occurs when water is channelled across unprotected land (up to 30cm) and washes away the soil along the drainage lines.

narrower.label: rill erosion
narrower.definition: The removal of soil by surface flows that either form small, shallow channels or streamlets - neither deeper than 30 cm. Because of its higher surface-flow velocities, rill erosion has a greater capacity than sheet erosion to remove and transport soil.

definitions.text: The removal of soil by surface flows that either form small, shallow channels or streamlets - neither deeper than 30 cm. Because of its higher surface-flow velocities, rill erosion has a greater capacity than sheet erosion to remove and transport soil.

narrower.label: sheet erosion
narrower.definition: Sheet erosion, which is a uniform removal of soil in thin layers from sloping land, occurs where the velocity of surface run-off is about 0.3 to 0.6 meters per second.

definitions.text: Sheet erosion, which is a uniform removal of soil in thin layers from sloping land, occurs where the velocity of surface run-off is about 0.3 to 0.6 meters per second.

narrower.label: splash erosion
narrower.definition: The spattering of small soil particles caused by the impact of raindrops on wet soils. The loosened and spattered particles may or may not be subsequently removed by surface runoff.

narrower.label: soil pollution
narrower.definition: Soil pollution refers to the presence in the soil of a chemical or substance out of place and/or present at a higher than normal concentration that has adverse effects on any non-targeted organism.

narrower.label: perfluoroalkyl acids
narrower.definition: The perfluoroalkyl acids (PFAA) are a family of perfluorinated chemicals that consist of a carbon backbone typically 4–14 in length and a charged functional moiety (primarily carboxylate, sulfonate, or phosphonate).

narrower.label: polychlorinated biphenyls
narrower.definition: PCB are toxic and can cause serious health effects in humans and animals, including reproductive impairment and immune system dysfunctions. Once in the environment, PCB enter the food chain. PCBs are toxic to wildlife, including fish, killing them at higher doses and causing spawning failures at lower doses.

narrower.label: polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons
narrower.definition: A class of chemicals that result from burning coal, oil, gas, wood, garbage, or tobacco. They bind to or form small particles in the air. High heat when cooking meat and other foods will also form PAHs.

narrower.label: soil sealing
narrower.definition: Permanent covering of the soil surface with impermeable artificial materials, leading to non-reversible loss of soil and most of its ecosystem services

narrower.label: soil sealing consistence
narrower.definition: The sealing consistence of soil describes the resistance of the soil to the formation of a surface crust or compacted layer, which can impede water infiltration and root penetration. This phenomenon typically occurs in fine-textured soils, such as clays and silts, where the particles are tightly bound, leading to a hardened surface layer upon wetting and drying. Sealing consistence affects water movement and can lead to surface runoff and erosion in agricultural soils. Source: Soil Science Society of America (SSSA). (2008). Glossary of Soil Science Terms. Soil Science Society of America.

narrower.label: soil sealing thickness
narrower.definition: The sealing thickness refers to the depth of the compacted or sealed layer within the soil, which is typically a result of intense rainfall, drying, or tillage practices. This layer, which forms in fine-textured soils, can significantly reduce water infiltration and root growth, leading to reduced soil aeration and potential surface runoff. The sealing thickness property is crucial for understanding soil erosion risks and water management in agricultural systems. Source: Pagliai, M., & Vignozzi, N. (2002). Soil Structure and Soil Quality: A Review of the State of the Art. Agriculture, Ecosystems & Environment, 88(3), 77-86.

narrower.label: waterlogging
narrower.definition: The state of land in which the water table is located at or near the soil surface, affecting crop yields.
